title: After-action: cascading throttle + circuit-breaker trip during peak traffic spike
creator: Aisha Khan
description: Summary: On 2026-03-09 16:12 UTC we observed a cross-region latency and error-rate incident that caused partial SLO misses for the EU and APAC customer tiers. The incident originated from a traffic spike to a small subset of public API keys that triggered aggressive token-level throttling in the edge proxies. That throttling increased request latency, causing KV cache eviction pressure on the serving nodes and a delayed autoscaling response. As latency rose, downstream circuit-breakers (configured per-region) tripped; fallback routing pushed additional load into healthy regions, producing a cascading series of throttles and partial load-shedding that lasted ~27 minutes. Impact: 14% of requests returned 5xx or 429 globally during the window; EU region saw a 22% SLO miss for p95 latency across the 30-minute window. This ticket documents the after-action analysis and the set of follow-up mitigations to avoid recurrence.
timeline: 2026-03-09 16:08 UTC - Traffic increase begins: marketing campaign warm-up caused burst from a handful of keys (ratio ~8x normal for 3 API keys).
2026-03-09 16:12 UTC - Edge proxies enforce token-level throttling for offending keys; error rates start climbing in EU-edge clusters.
2026-03-09 16:15 UTC - Serving nodes in eu-west experienced KV cache pressure; median generation latency increases from 85ms to 420ms for affected hosts.
2026-03-09 16:18 UTC - Regional circuit-breakers for eu-west trip due to elevated latency and error budget exhaustion. Traffic routed to us-east and ap-south.
2026-03-09 16:20 UTC - us-east begins to see increased tail latency; automatic load-shedding policy on dedicated pools activates (30% of requests dropped to maintain SLOs for higher-tier customers).
2026-03-09 16:25 UTC - On-call (Liam) opens incident, temporarily relaxes token-level throttling thresholds and scales up a dedicated pool + unpins a cache shard.
2026-03-09 16:35 UTC - Circuit-breakers gradually close; error rates return to baseline by 16:39 UTC. Post-incident monitoring continues through 17:30 UTC.
root_causes: Token-level throttling was overly strict for a low-cardinality burst: threshold used a fixed tokens-per-minute heuristic that didn't account for short bursts from known partner keys.
Circuit-breaker configuration used short windowed error budgets which tripped quickly during transient latency spikes instead of using adaptive decay backoff.
Autoscaling policy for dedicated pools is configured with a conservative cooldown and step size; scaling lagged the initial latency increase and failed to absorb failover load quickly.
KV cache eviction behavior was sensitive to request fanout; the cache strategy didn't prioritize hot prefixes for the observed workload, increasing tail latency under pressure.
mitigations_performed: Emergency actions during incident: relaxed token-throttle for identified keys, manual scale-up of two dedicated pools in eu-west, and temporarily reduced circuit-breaker aggressiveness to allow graceful degradation.
Rolled a hotfix to edge config to whitelist partner keys from token-throttle while preserving global quota accounting (short-term mitigation).
Unpinned and redistributed a cache shard that had become a hotspot; this reduced per-host KV misses by ~40% in the affected cohort.
postmortem_summary: This was a classic cascade: conservative per-layer protections (token throttles, tight circuit-breaker windows, conservative autoscaling) combined with a low-cardinality burst led to a multi-region failover that amplified load onto remaining capacity. While each protection behaved as configured, their composition created worse global outcomes than permitting short-term throttling tolerances or faster autoscale responses. The recommended long-term fix is to make the stack aware of burst characteristics (hot-key detection + short-term burst allowances), make circuit-breakers adapt to transient spikes, and improve autoscaler responsiveness for failover scenarios.
action_items: ENG-8342-A1: Implement hot-key detection in edge proxies and add a 'short-burst' throttle bucket (owner: Priya Desai, due: 2026-04-07) - measure: reduce throttled requests for transient partner bursts by >90%.

ENG-8342-A2: Change circuit-breaker policy to use a hybrid window+adaptive-decay model and add canary thresholds for regional failover (owner: Marco Liu, due: 2026-04-14) - measure: reduce false-positive trips in controlled load tests to <1%.

ENG-8342-A3: Tune autoscaler for dedicated pools: lower cooldown from 300s to 90s for failover-triggered scaling, add an emergency fast-path to add small burst capacity (owner: Elena Garcia, due: 2026-04-21) - measure: scale recovery time <60s under simulated failover load.

ENG-8342-A4: Rework KV cache eviction policy to pin hot prefixes for 10s windows during spikes and add telemetry to surface prefix hotness (owner: Noah Reed, due: 2026-04-28) - measure: p95 latency reduction for affected hosts by 30% in replay tests.

ENG-8342-A5: Update runbooks and incident playbooks: define 'burst whitelist' process for low-risk partner keys, and add explicit steps for circuit-breaker rollback and controlled reroute (owner: SRE Team, due: 2026-03-24) - measure: runbook verified in next incident runbook drill.
ENG-8342-A6: Post-incident client communications: send summary to affected customers and post incident notes in status.redwood.ai (owner: Support Ops - Maya Patel, due: 2026-03-15).
